Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After settling ...), mid-sentence blank; the painter is the right subject
items.passage: Korean painter Kim Whanki devoted much of the 1950s to depicting moons, mountains, and plum blossoms, motifs rooted in traditional Korean art. After relocating to New York in 1963, ______ covering entire canvases with thousands of tiny dots, each one enclosed in a square of color.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Kim’s painting style became purely abstract, the artist eventually
Kim developed a purely abstract style, eventually
a purely abstract style emerged in Kim’s work as he began
it was in a purely abstract style that Kim began
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “After relocating to New York in 1963,” describes someone who moved to the city: the painter. Choice B places “Kim” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Kim moved to New York and then developed a purely abstract style.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Kim’s painting style,” not Kim, so the sentence illogically says that a painting style relocated to New York in 1963.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the style
C.why_wrong: “A purely abstract style” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the style, rather than the painter, relocated to New York.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has nothing it can logically describe; Kim appears only later, inside the clause.

items.notes: Subject: Korean painter Kim Whanki, who moved to New York in 1963 and turned to all-over dot paintings (arts, painting). Real painter; facts kept general (traditional motifs such as moons, mountains and plum blossoms in the 1950s; New York from 1963; canvases of dots, each set in a square). No moon jars, which a live FSS item uses. Band 6 as dfbf5d33 and d2b81427: plain agent key after a preposition + gerund opener, mid-sentence blank whose options run into a participial phrase. Recipes P, W, E (all three distinct). Every option is grammatical on its own and keeps the same facts.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. As dfbf5d33: plain agent key after a preposition + gerund opener, mid-sentence blank running into a participial phrase; foils P (Kim’s painting style), W (a purely abstract style) and E (it was ... that).

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener about a property (Ranging from ... to ...), passage-final blank; the right subject is “the suggested causes of the lights,” built on the obvious noun
items.passage: Since the early 1980s, residents of the Hessdalen valley in central Norway have reported luminous white or yellow spheres drifting above the surrounding hills, some hovering motionless for more than an hour. Ranging from charged dust to radioactive gas, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the lights have many suggested causes, none of which has yet been confirmed.
it remains unclear which of the suggested causes of the lights is correct.
the suggested causes of the lights have yet to be confirmed by researchers.
researchers have suggested many causes of the lights but have yet to confirm any.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Ranging from charged dust to radioactive gas,” describes the possible causes of the lights: dust and gas are proposed explanations, not the lights themselves. Choice C places “the suggested causes of the lights” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the suggested causes are what range from charged dust to radioactive gas.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the lights
A.why_wrong: “The lights” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the lights themselves range from charged dust to radioactive gas.

B.recipe: expletive opener (E): it remains unclear which
B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has nothing it can logically describe; the suggested causes appear only later, inside the clause.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the agent, researchers
D.why_wrong: “Researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the researchers range from charged dust to radioactive gas.

items.notes: Subject: the Hessdalen lights, unexplained balls of light over a valley in central Norway (science, atmospheric physics). Real phenomenon; facts kept general (reports since the early 1980s, white or yellow lights that can hover for over an hour, proposed causes including charged dust and radioactive radon gas). No researchers named. Reviewer rebuild for band 7 on the setting of band7 section 5: the opener states a property (a range of causes), so the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the suggested causes of the lights), and the obvious noun itself (the lights) and the agent (researchers) are the foils, with an expletive. Options 12 to 14 words, each stating the same facts.
band7_moves: property key (band-7 file, section 3 move 7): the right subject is “the lights of Hessdalen,” a noun phrase built on the place noun that the passage keeps as its topic
the hardest foil, A, starts with that obvious noun and keeps every fact, so it reads naturally until the student asks what actually glows
B and D hold the lights inside an it-clause and a nominalisation (E and N, as in 2bca654a); three distinct recipes
two-part opener (two participles joined by and); passage-final blank; options 16 to 20 words, all grammatical, same facts

fixes: rebuilt for band 7: the opener described the lights’ look (Glowing ... hovering ...), so the key was the obvious noun and the valley foil died on one fact; the opener is now a property claim (Ranging from charged dust to radioactive gas), the key “the suggested causes of the lights,” the foils the lights (W), an expletive (E) and researchers (agent W); options cut from 19 or 20 words to 12 to 14; the look of the lights moved into sentence 1; subtype, explanation, distractors and notes rewritten
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Before the fix band 6 (the key was the obvious noun, the lights). Now the R3 setting of band7 section 5: a property opener whose right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun, with the obvious noun itself as a foil that keeps every fact, plus an agent foil (researchers) and an expletive; same recipe family as 2bca654a (it-cleft, nominalised and passive foils).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a long plural subject holding a relative clause with its own finite verb (some of which are ...)
items.passage: In 1969, the Allende meteorite disintegrated over the Mexican state of Chihuahua, scattering more than two tons of fragments. The pale, irregular inclusions embedded in these fragments, some of which are older than any rock that formed on Earth, ______ researchers a rare glimpse of the earliest solid materials in the solar system.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “The pale, irregular inclusions,” and everything up to the blank describes those inclusions, including the clause “some of which are older than any rock that formed on Earth.” The sentence still needs a main verb for that subject. Choice D supplies the finite verb “have given,” so the sentence says what the inclusions have done.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
A.why_wrong: The participle “giving” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, so the sentence would have no main verb for “The pale, irregular inclusions.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to give” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
C.why_wrong: The phrase “having given” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb for its subject.

items.notes: Subject: the Allende meteorite, which fell in Chihuahua, Mexico, in 1969, and its calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (science, planetary science). Real event; facts kept general (more than two tons of fragments, pale inclusions about 4.57 billion years old, older than any Earth rock). Band 6 as a75d5984: canonical set {finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle}; the head noun is held apart from the blank by 16 words of a participial phrase and a relative clause whose own verb (are) can make the clause feel complete. Different frame from the live w5b2_03 (a participial phrase and one partitive relative clause, not two stacked relative clauses).

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official item, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as a75d5984, the head 16 words before the blank behind a participial phrase and a partitive relative clause with its own finite verb (are).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: plural head (turtle ships) behind a relative clause and an appositive full of singular nouns, with a singular verb (appears) inside
items.passage: Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin repeatedly defeated larger Japanese fleets between 1592 and 1598. The turtle ships that Yi commanded, a design whose earliest documented mention appears in a royal chronicle from 1413, ______ protected by a curved roof that, according to some accounts, bristled with iron spikes to keep enemy sailors from boarding.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “turtle ships.” The clause “that Yi commanded” and the phrase beginning “a design whose” describe those ships. Choice A supplies the plural verb “were,” which agrees with “ships.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” agrees with the nearby singular nouns, such as “design” or “chronicle,” not with the plural subject “ships.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” does not agree with the plural subject “ships.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” does not agree with the plural subject “ships.”

items.notes: Subject: the Korean turtle ships (geobukseon) used by admiral Yi Sun-sin against Japanese fleets in 1592 to 1598, first mentioned in the Joseon annals in 1413 (history). Real; facts kept general (covered roof; iron spikes hedged with “according to some accounts”). Skeleton differs from earlier band-7 R1_be items: relative clause straight after the head, then an appositive with a whose-clause, not “The X of Y, which ...”.
band7_moves: plural head behind singular nouns (band-7 file, section 3 move 5): Yi, design, mention, chronicle sit between “ships” and the blank
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number (move 4): “whose earliest known mention appears,” so the singular sounds right twice
20 run words after the blank; run of 40 words counting the blank
options unchanged: three wrong-number forms in three tenses

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: The dc645172 setting: plural head (turtle ships) behind a relative clause and an appositive holding three singular nouns (design, mention, chronicle) and its own singular finite verb (appears), 18 words after the blank; options wrong number in three tenses as 8a9d2f4e.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate (placed ... and ___) after a 16-word subject holding a relative clause with its own infinitive
items.passage: In 1934, two researchers at the University of Cologne who hoped to accelerate the processing of photographic film placed an ultrasound transducer in a tank of developer and ______ minuscule dots on the film, the first recorded evidence of sonoluminescence, light emitted by collapsing bubbles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “two researchers” has two verbs joined by “and”: the researchers “placed” a transducer in the tank and then did something else. The blank needs a second finite verb that matches “placed.” Choice B supplies the past tense verb “found,” so the sentence correctly says that the researchers placed the transducer and found the dots.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
A.why_wrong: The participle “finding” does not match the finite verb “placed,” so “and finding” cannot form the second part of the compound predicate.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to find” does not match “placed,” so the sentence would have no second main verb after “and.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
D.why_wrong: The phrase “having found” is nonfinite, so it cannot join “placed” as the second main verb.

items.notes: Subject: the 1934 discovery of sonoluminescence at the University of Cologne, when an ultrasound transducer in a tank of photographic developer left dots on film (science, physics). Real; facts kept general (researchers unnamed: they were H. Frenzel and H. Schultes; hoped to speed up developing; dots traced to light from bubbles). Band 6 as b74f676f: the finite key matches the tense of the first verb; the subject is lengthened by a relative clause with its own infinitive (to accelerate), so “to find” can look parallel to it. No participle stands before the blank, so “and finding” has nothing to pair with. Skeleton differs from b74f676f (no dash interrupter before “and”).

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official item, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as b74f676f, the second verb of a compound predicate after a 16-word subject whose relative clause holds an infinitive (to accelerate) that makes “to find” look parallel.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, plain plural (stones) plus plural possessor (frogs’) before a plural possessed noun (bodies)
items.passage: Goliath frogs, native to Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, are the largest living frogs. In 2019, researchers reported that these frogs excavate nesting pools along riverbanks, sometimes relocating ______ bodies to shelter the eggs from the current.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: stone’s weighing more than half as much as the frogs’
stones weighing more than half as much as the frog’s
stones weighing more than half as much as the frogs
stones weighing more than half as much as the frogs’
items.explanation: The first noun is a plain plural: the frogs relocate more than one stone, so “stones” needs no apostrophe. The second noun is a plural possessive: the bodies belong to the frogs, so “frogs’” is needed. Choice D is the only one that uses both forms.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Stone’s” is a singular possessive, but nothing belongs to a stone; the context needs the plural noun “stones.”

B.why_wrong: “Frog’s” is a singular possessive, but the bodies belong to many frogs; one frog cannot have several bodies.

C.why_wrong: “Frogs” is a plain plural, so nothing shows that the bodies belong to the frogs; the plural possessive “frogs’” is needed.

items.notes: Subject: Goliath frogs that clear nest pools along riverbanks and move heavy stones (science, biology). Real, reported in a 2019 field study in Cameroon; facts kept general (no researchers named; stones weighing more than half a frog’s weight, moved to shelter the eggs). Each wrong option has one wrong slot.
band7_moves: two slots with a plural possessor (band-7 file, section 3 move 9), as in 2784cbaf
the possessor is separated from the plain plural by an 8-word participial phrase, so the two slots must be judged separately
without the apostrophe, “frogs own” reads as subject + verb, a garden path rather than a plain spelling slip
the possessed noun “bodies” is plural, so only the plural possessor fits; frame differs from the earlier band-7 items (no “X on/of Ys’”)

fixes: dropped “own” before “bodies”, so the no-apostrophe foil is a plain missing apostrophe instead of reading as a subject and verb (“frogs own bodies”); B and C why_wrong updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: 2784cbaf is band 7 because its possessor is generic (“objects’”) with a singular “an object” earlier pulling toward “object’s”; here “these frogs” and the plural “bodies” fix both slots from adjacent words. A singular pull (generic “the frog’s body”) would make two answers defensible, so it stays a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head (search) behind a possessive and a set-off phrase full of plurals (lanes, stairways)
items.passage: In Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami’s 1987 film Where Is the Friend’s House?, a schoolboy realizes that he has accidentally taken a classmate’s notebook home. The boy’s search for his friend’s house, through the winding lanes and steep stairways of a neighboring village, ______ up most of the film.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “search”; the phrase “through the winding lanes and steep stairways of a neighboring village” only describes where the search goes. Choice A supplies the singular verb “takes,” which agrees with “search.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “take” agrees with the nearby plural nouns “lanes” and “stairways,” not with the singular subject “search.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are taking” does not agree with the singular subject “search.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have taken” does not agree with the singular subject “search.”

items.notes: Subject: Abbas Kiarostami’s film Where Is the Friend’s House? (1987), in which a boy tries to return a classmate’s notebook in a neighboring village (arts, film). Real film; facts kept general. Medium as 2.20 and 2.22: a singular head with a possessive before it and a set-off phrase holding two plural nouns between head and blank (15 words).

fixes: trimmed “young” (batch medium passages ran above CB’s median)
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun for a singular thing (a bachi), with plural nouns (strings) on both sides
items.passage: The shamisen, a three-stringed Japanese lute, has a square wooden body covered with tightly stretched animal skin. Its silk strings are played with a large, fan-shaped plectrum called a bachi; because ______ can strike the skin as well as the strings, each note begins with a distinctive percussive snap.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun in the blank refers to the thing that strikes the skin as well as the strings: the plectrum, “a bachi.” Because “a bachi” is singular, the singular pronoun “it” is needed.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent “a bachi”; it seems to point to the strings, which cannot strike themselves.

B.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two things, but only one thing, the bachi, strikes the skin and the strings.

D.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” does not agree with the singular antecedent “a bachi.”

items.notes: Subject: the shamisen and its large plectrum, the bachi, which hits the skin-covered body as well as the strings (arts, music). Real instrument; facts kept general. Medium as 2.15: the antecedent is a singular thing, with the plural “strings” just before it and again after the blank. The verb after the blank (can strike) does not show number, so the choice rests on the antecedent alone. No person appears (reviewer made the bachi sentence passive), so “they” cannot be read as a singular they for a performer.

fixes: “A performer plays its silk strings” made passive (“Its silk strings are played”): with a singular person in the passage, “they” was defensible as a singular they for the performer, who does strike the skin; now “they” can point only to the strings; notes updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, quantifier subject: “Each of the first six digits ...” takes a singular verb
items.passage: In the fifth century CE, Chinese mathematician Zu Chongzhi proposed the fraction 355/113 as an approximation of pi. Each of the first six digits after the decimal point in this fraction’s value ______ the corresponding digit of pi, a remarkable result for its time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “Each,” which is singular; the phrase “of the first six digits after the decimal point in this fraction’s value” only says which items are meant. Choice B supplies the singular verb “matches,” which agrees with “Each.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “match” agrees with the nearby plural noun “digits,” not with the singular subject “Each.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are matching” does not agree with the singular subject “Each.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have matched” does not agree with the singular subject “Each.”

items.notes: Subject: Zu Chongzhi’s fifth-century fraction 355/113 for pi, which is correct to six decimal places (science, mathematics). Real; facts kept general (3.1415929 against 3.1415926). Medium as 2.23: a quantifier head (“Each of”) with a plural noun right after it and 13 words between head and blank. Lexical verb options in the R1_lex pattern.

fixes: trimmed the tail “for calculations performed with counting rods” to “for its time” (length); notes updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense, simple past: dated span in the previous sentence (From 1936 to 1966) and a present perfect reporting verb (Historians have noted that ...)
items.passage: From 1936 to 1966, postal worker Victor Hugo Green published The Negro Motorist Green Book, a guide to hotels, restaurants, and gas stations that would serve Black travelers under segregation. Historians have noted that Green ______ on fellow postal employees to gather listings for the guide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that Green published the guide “From 1936 to 1966,” so his work on it is a completed action in the past. Choice D supplies the simple past tense verb “relied,” which correctly places his reliance on other postal employees in that period.

A.recipe: present simple where past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present tense “relies” suggests that Green relies on postal employees today, but the guide was published from 1936 to 1966.

B.why_wrong: The future tense “will rely” suggests an action still to come, but Green’s work on the guide ended long ago.

C.why_wrong: The present progressive “is relying” suggests an action happening now, not one completed decades ago.

items.notes: Subject: Victor Hugo Green’s Green Book (1936 to 1966) and the postal network that helped him collect listings (social science, history). Real; facts kept general. Medium as 2.12: the dated cue sits in the previous sentence and the blank follows a present perfect reporting verb (“Historians have noted that”), which tempts a present form. Only one past form is offered.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense, past perfect: an earlier past before “By the time it reached scholars”
items.passage: In 1881, a farmer near the village of Bakhshali, in present-day Pakistan, unearthed a mathematical treatise on birch bark, one that uses a dot as a symbol for zero. By the time it reached scholars, the fragile manuscript ______ into approximately seventy loose leaves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “By the time it reached scholars” sets a point in the past, and the manuscript’s coming apart happened before that point. Choice A supplies the past perfect verb “had separated,” which correctly shows an action completed before another past event.

B.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: The present tense “separates” does not fit the past time frame set by “By the time it reached scholars.”

C.why_wrong: The future tense “will separate” suggests an action still to come, but the manuscript came apart before it reached scholars in the past.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “is separating” suggests an action happening now, not one completed before a past event.

items.notes: Subject: the Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark mathematical text found by a farmer in 1881 near Mardan, with a dot used for zero (science, history of mathematics). Real; facts kept general (about 70 fragmentary leaves). Medium version of the earlier-past cell: the cue is a “By the time” clause in the same sentence, as in 2.8 but with the blank in the main clause. Simple past is not offered (the brief’s rule for past perfect keys), so no second option can be defended.

fixes: options checked (batch note): same shape as 2.8 and 1.24, no simple past, and none of the present, future or progressive forms fits “By the time it reached scholars”; verb changed from “broken” to “separated” in all four options (a manuscript breaking “into seventy leaves” is an odd collocation for pages); trimmed to 44 words (“one that employs” to “that uses”, dropped “many of them severely damaged”); explanation and why_wrong updated
relative clause kept next to its head: “a mathematical treatise on birch bark, one that uses a dot as a symbol for zero”
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement in a relative clause: “which” refers back to a singular title; options carry the predicate noun, which must agree too
items.passage: Venetian-born writer Christine de Pizan was among the earliest European women to earn a living through writing. In 1405 she completed The Book of the City of Ladies, which ______ to women from history and mythology whose accomplishments male authors had frequently dismissed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The relative pronoun “which” refers back to The Book of the City of Ladies, a single work. Choice C supplies the singular verb “is” and the singular noun phrase “an allegorical tribute,” both of which agree with that singular antecedent.

A.recipe: wrong number, verb and predicate noun plural
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” and plural noun “tributes” do not agree with the singular antecedent of “which,” the single book.

B.recipe: wrong number verb with singular predicate noun
B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular antecedent of “which,” the single book.

D.recipe: wrong number, past, predicate noun plural
D.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” and plural noun “tributes” do not agree with the singular antecedent, the single book.

items.notes: Subject: Christine de Pizan’s The Book of the City of Ladies (1405) (literature). Real; facts kept general (born in Venice, among the first European women to live by writing, the book honours women of history and myth against male writers’ dismissals). Medium as 2.18: relative “which” whose antecedent is the title just before it; option shape copied from 2.18 (verb plus predicate noun). The plural nouns after the blank (women, accomplishments, authors) tempt the plural.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense, simple present: a general fact, parallel with the present verbs “is” in the same passage
items.passage: Situated near the center of the Milky Way, the molecular cloud Sagittarius B2 is one of the richest known reservoirs of complex organic compounds. Among the many chemicals it ______ is ethyl formate, a substance that contributes to the flavor of raspberries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes the cloud as it is now (“is one of the richest known reservoirs”), and the sentence with the blank continues in the present (“is ethyl formate”). Choice B supplies the simple present verb “contains,” which fits this present-day description.

A.recipe: conditional or exotic compound: future perfect
A.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have contained” refers to a point in the future, but the passage describes what the cloud contains now.

C.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
C.why_wrong: The past perfect “had contained” refers to a time before another past event, but the passage describes the cloud in the present.

D.why_wrong: The past progressive “was containing” refers to an ongoing past action, which does not fit the present description.

items.notes: Subject: the gas cloud Sagittarius B2 near the galactic center, in which astronomers detected ethyl formate, a compound that contributes to the flavor of raspberries (science, astronomy). Real; facts kept general (detected in 2009). Easy as 1.1: present-day description with distractors from three other tense families.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense, simple present: how a device works, parallel with “accumulate” and “jumps” in the same sentence
items.passage: In a Kelvin water dropper, an apparatus devised by physicist William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) in 1867, two narrow streams of water drip through metal rings into separate collecting cans. As the drops ______, opposite electric charges accumulate in the cans until a spark eventually jumps between them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage explains how the device works in general, using present tense verbs (“drip,” “accumulate,” “jumps”). Choice D supplies the simple present verb “fall,” which matches those verbs.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “fell” does not match the present tense verbs “accumulate” and “jumps” that describe how the device works.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had fallen” refers to a time before another past event, but the passage describes the device’s operation in the present.

C.recipe: conditional or exotic compound: future perfect
C.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have fallen” refers to a point in the future, which does not fit a general description of how the device works.

items.notes: Subject: the Kelvin water dropper (1867), in which dripping water charges two cans until a spark jumps (science, physics). Real; facts kept general. Easy as 1.3: the blank verb must match present verbs in the same sentence. Distinct from the live Kelvin tide-predicting machine item.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun for a named woman (Irma Stern)
items.passage: In 1917, South African painter Irma Stern met German artist Max Pechstein in Berlin. Pechstein admired Stern’s bold colors and expressive brushwork, and he encouraged ______ to exhibit her paintings, which were shown at a Berlin gallery two years later.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person Pechstein encouraged to exhibit “her paintings” is Irma Stern, a single woman. Choice A supplies the singular pronoun “her,” which agrees with that antecedent.

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “them” does not agree with the singular antecedent, Irma Stern; it seems to point to her colors, which cannot exhibit paintings.

C.recipe: wrong number and kind: it for a person
C.why_wrong: The pronoun “it” refers to a thing, not to a person such as Stern.
